suggestions.rationale: Paravalvular leak is an uncommon but clinically important residual or complication after prosthetic heart-valve replacement and can produce hemolysis and hemolytic anemia. Meta-analytic evidence on paravalvular-leak treatment identifies hemolysis as a serious clinical consequence. This supports a treatment-complication pathway only when a post-replacement paravalvular leak and objective hemolysis are documented; valve replacement by itself is not sufficient to attribute an individual anemia to the procedure.

pathwayIntelligence.causalChain: Heart-valve replacement → documented paravalvular leak around the prosthesis → mechanical red-cell hemolysis → diagnosed hemolytic anemia.
developmentQuestions: Is a paravalvular leak documented after the valve replacement by echocardiography or other appropriate cardiac imaging?
Do laboratory findings support hemolysis, such as reduced hemoglobin with elevated LDH, reduced haptoglobin, reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, or schistocytes as clinically applicable?
Did the anemia and hemolysis begin or materially worsen after the documented paravalvular leak developed?
Did correction or reduction of the leak improve the hemolysis or anemia, if an intervention occurred?

Which alternative causes of anemia or hemolysis, including bleeding, nutritional deficiency, kidney disease, marrow disease, medication effects, infection, or other mechanical causes, should be addressed?
issuesToResolve: The relationship requires a documented paravalvular leak and objective hemolysis; prosthetic-valve status alone does not establish hemolytic anemia.
Anemia phenotype, chronology, imaging, hemolysis markers, treatment response, and competing causes require individual review.

evidenceGaps: Operative records identifying the prosthetic valve and replacement procedure
Echocardiography or other imaging documenting a post-replacement paravalvular leak
Laboratory evidence characterizing anemia and hemolysis
Clinical chronology and any response after leak closure or valve re-intervention
Qualified cardiology/hematology assessment excluding other important causes of anemia or hemolysis

sourceReferences.citation: Improta R et al. Transcatheter or surgical treatment of paravalvular leaks: A meta-analysis of 13 studies and 2003 patients. Int J Cardiol Heart Vasc. 2024. PMID 40103841
sourceReferences.note: Meta-analysis describes significant paravalvular leak as a rare but serious complication of heart-valve replacement associated with heart failure and hemolysis. Supports a documented leak-to-hemolysis pathway, not anemia attribution from valve replacement alone.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 40103841; abstract: significant paravalvular leak after heart-valve replacement can cause symptomatic heart failure and hemolysis
